Split-population (cure) model of recidivism

Source: R/spcure.R
spcure.Rd

Asks two questions that an ordinary survival model runs together: what share of people released will ever be reconvicted, and how soon those who are reconvicted fail. A Kaplan-Meier curve of time to reconviction levels off well above 0: many released people never fail, however long they are followed. Schmidt and Witte (1989) model this with a split population: each person would eventually fail with chance delta = 1 / (1 + exp(-x'gamma)) (the "fail" part), and the time to failure of those who would fail follows a distribution with scale exp(x'beta) (the "time" part): a Weibull with a common shape, an exponential, or a lognormal (log time normal with mean x'beta and a common standard deviation sigma). A person followed to time t without failing contributes 1 - delta + delta S(t), one who failed at t contributes delta f(t). The parameters are estimated by maximum likelihood (quasi-Newton steps with the analytic gradient) with standard errors from the inverse of the Hessian.

Usage

spcure(time, event, x = NULL, dist = "weibull", level = 0.95, maxit = 500)

Arguments

time

The time each person was followed to failure or to the end of follow-up: positive numbers.

event

Whether each time is a failure (1 or TRUE) or the end of follow-up (0 or FALSE); failures and censored times both.

x

NULL or the covariates of both parts: a numeric matrix, a data frame or list of numeric columns, or one numeric vector, one row per person.

dist

The time to failure: "weibull", "exp" or "lognormal".

level

The confidence level of the Wald intervals: one number strictly between 0 and 1.

maxit

The quasi-Newton steps: one whole number from 1.

Value

An object of class spcure, a list: coef, one row per parameter (part: "fail", "time" or "shape"; term, est, se, lo, hi, z, p); fit, a named vector (loglik, aic, iter, conv (1 when converged), pfail); dist; and n.

Details

The two parts are told apart by the long right tail of the follow-up: if everyone is followed only briefly, a low share failing and slow failure look alike and the estimates are unstable (large standard errors). pfail is the mean of delta over the people, the estimated share who would ever fail.

References

Schmidt, P. and Witte, A. D. (1989). Predicting criminal recidivism using 'split population' survival time models. Journal of Econometrics, 40(1), 141-159. doi:10.1016/0304-4076(89)90034-1

Maltz, M. D. (1984). Recidivism. Academic Press, Orlando.

See also

kmrec() for the Kaplan-Meier curve.

Examples

set.seed(10)
n <- 600
prior <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.4)
fail <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-0.5 + 1.2 * prior))
tt <- ifelse(fail == 1, rweibull(n, 1.3, 300), Inf)
cens <- runif(n, 365, 1500)
r <- spcure(pmin(tt, cens), as.numeric(tt <= cens), data.frame(prior))
r
